newsitem.title: FRANCE: French GAN boss a political sacrifice -Socialists.
newsitem.headline: French GAN boss a political sacrifice -Socialists.

text.p: France's opposition Socialist Party accused the government on Wednesday of settling political scores in demanding that the head of state-owned insurer GAN, resign in the wake of a high-profile bank privatisation debacle.

The Socialists, gaining ground fast in opinion polls against Prime Minister Alain Juppe's unpopular centre-right government, said attempts to privatise the GAN banking subsidiary CIC were inappropriate and said the GAN/CIC group should be kept intact.

The government said last week it was abandoning a tender to privatise CIC in the face of resistance from staff and regional politicians and called on GAN chairman Jean-Jacques Bonnaud to quit on the grounds he failed to help promote the sell-off.
Bonnaud crossed swords with the prime minister earlier this year when Juppe attempted to place a close advisor at the head of CIC.
Bonnaud had his way and appointed Bernard Yoncourt head of the regional banking group after Juppe backed down amid a storm of media controversy.
"The government of Mr Alain Juppe has yet again demonstrated its mismanagement of privatisations," the Socialist Party said.

"It weighed up the failure of its actions and backed off (on the CIC sale). It is now taking disciplinary action and calling for the resignation of GAN chairman Mr Jean-Jacques Bonnaud, and in the same blow the departure of CIC chairman Bernard Yoncourt as well," it said in a statement.
"This is a political settling of scores, and undoubtedly a precursor to a takeover of some other kind with other bosses in charge of privatising," it added.

Bonnaud, who faces the prospect of being fired next week, is waging a defensive campaign in the French media, saying standing down at the government's behest would be as good as an admission that he was at fault.

Finance Minister Jean Arthuis, who is currently in Japan with President Jacques Chirac, called off the privatisation of the CIC last week amid opposition from CIC staff and mounting criticism from regional politicans -- and after attracting only one eligible offer, from French bank BNP.

"The Socialist Party deems the privatisation inappropriate," said the statement from the opposition party. "The Socialist Party wants the decentralised structure and the integrity of the GAN/CIC group preserved."

"It (Socialists) reiterates its opposition to the current process of privatisations, which are inefficient and whose sole aim is to finf the financial resources to bridge the gap in public deficits," the Socialist Party statement added.
Arthuis says he is determined to privatise CIC but scrapped the recent sell-off tender to allow more time to reflect.

CIC boss Yoncourt infuriated Arthuis by saying at a delicate stage in the middle of the privatisation tender in October that a takeover could spell the "death" of his bank, a group of 11 regional banks which prides itself on its close relations with bid and medium sized businesses at regional and local level.
